explanation: In Vietnam, hugging is usually reserved for close friends or relatives, so hugging someone you have just met or an acquaintance at a social gathering can feel overly familiar. Standard greetings rely on a smile, nod, handshake or verbal 'Xin chào', with deference shown to elders. Public displays of affection, including hugging, are generally kept modest, especially in traditional or rural settings.
local_tip: At a gathering, greet the oldest person first with a smile and slight nod or handshake, and only hug if a close friend or relative initiates it.
regional_note: Rural and more traditional areas tend to be more reserved about public hugging than urban settings, and younger generations may be more relaxed among close peers.

also_check.note: The wai greeting is standard; hugging is common among friends but avoid touching the head or hugging monks.
Bowing is the norm; hugging is uncommon in formal or first-time greetings and reserved for close relationships.
La bise (cheek kisses) or hugs among friends are common greetings, though handshakes suit formal or first meetings.
